references.text: God promises Abraham that Sarah will bear a son named Isaac and sets the time of birth (v. 21), which corresponds to the specific time mentioned in 21:2.
The Lord confirms that Sarah will bear a son at a set time and answers Sarah's laughter by saying nothing is impossible for the Lord.
Paul describes Abraham's faith in God's promise of a son, even though he and Sarah were 'dead' due to old age.
Paul explains that Abraham had two sons—one born of the slave woman according to the flesh, and the other of the free woman through the promise.
By faith, Sarah received power to conceive despite her old age because she considered Him faithful who had made the promise.
Confirms the fulfillment of the promise of a son in old age and identifies him as the promised heir.
Provides the necessary biological context that makes the birth in 21:2 a divine miracle.
Theological confirmation that Sarah's childbirth was the beginning of God's plan to make Abraham into a great nation.
The direct prophecy fulfilled in 21:2, which defines the event as a divine promise.
God's declaration that nothing is impossible for Him, serving as the theological basis for the miracle in 21:2.
Highlights the event as the result of patiently waiting on God's promise and confirms that God's timing was exact.
Identifies the event as a direct fulfillment of God's word of promise and emphasizes God's sovereign choice.
Creates a theological contrast between human doubt about possibility and God's actual fulfillment of the promise.
Explains the theological significance of the birth: Isaac is the chosen heir through whom the promise will be fulfilled.
Provides the theological basis for the promise: that Isaac will carry on a lineage that keeps to the Lord's way.
Illuminates the inner conviction of God's power that was necessary for the promise in 21:2 to be fulfilled.
